claim:
Let \(X=\ell_2-\ell_\infty\) be the real Day--James plane
\[
\|(s,t)\|_{2,\infty}=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{s^2+t^2},&st\ge0,\\
\max\{|s|,|t|\},&st\le0.
\end{cases}
\]
Its Dunkl--Williams constant is the known value \(DW(X)=2\sqrt2\), but the defining supremum is not attained: there are no nonzero distinct \(x,y\in X\) for which
\[
\frac{\|x\|+\|y\|}{\|x-y\|}
\left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|}-\frac{y}{\|y\|}\right\|
=2\sqrt2.
\]
Equivalently, in the unit-sphere formula
\[
DW(X)=
\sup_{\substack{u,v\in S_X\\u+v\ne0}}
\frac{\|u+v\|}
{\min_{0\le t\le1}\|(1-t)u+tv\|},
\]
every admissible quotient is strictly smaller than \(2\sqrt2\), although an explicit sequence of such quotients converges to \(2\sqrt2\).

correctness.rationale: The 2013 full text proves the unit-sphere representation, the Birkhoff-frame reduction, and the exact Day--James branch formulas. Every reduced extreme-point term is strictly below \(\sqrt2\): \(m(p_a,q_a)=1/a<\sqrt2\) on the first branch, \(m(p_a,q_a)<a+b<\sqrt2\) on the second, and \(m(w,p_a)=a(a+b)<\sqrt2\) on the corner branch. The axis and diagonal endpoints give \(m=1\). If a unit-sphere quotient equaled \(2\sqrt2\), the proof of the representation plus frame reduction would force an extreme point with \(M\ge\sqrt2\), contradicting those strict bounds. The displayed equal-level pair gives exact quotient \(2/a\), proving sharp approximation.
risks: The endpoint calculations are elementary additions to the source's open-arc reduction; they are stated explicitly in the proof.
The theorem concerns real scalars only.

value.rationale: The Day--James \(\ell_2-\ell_\infty\) plane is the canonical worked non-Hilbert example in the paper that introduced the modern calculation framework for the Dunkl--Williams constant. Showing that its sharp value is not attained identifies the geometric mechanism behind the classical computation: sharpness occurs only through a limiting transition at the Euclidean/sup seam. Nonattainment of a sharp finite-dimensional geometric constant is a substantive boundary fact, and the exact sequence \(2/a\to2\sqrt2\) gives a reusable test case for future attainment or stability questions.
risks: The result refines a classical exact calculation rather than introducing a new geometric constant.
No quantitative stability theorem for all near-maximizers is claimed.
